title: A small country opens its rice market: comparative advantage, the world price, imports and a tariff
scenario: Castrel and Ostavia are invented countries. In one day, a worker in Castrel can produce either 4 tons of rice or 8 bolts of cloth, and a worker in Ostavia can produce either 6 tons of rice or 6 bolts of cloth. Castrel is a small country: its trade does not change the world price of rice. In Castrel, the domestic market for rice is competitive, with straight-line demand and supply curves, and without trade the price is \$7 a ton.

table.caption: Tons of rice demanded and supplied per day in Castrel at each price (invented data for practice)

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Calculate the opportunity cost of 1 ton of rice in each country, and identify which country has the comparative advantage in rice.

rubric.point: Opportunity cost of 1 ton of rice: 2 bolts of cloth in Castrel (8 ÷ 4) and 1 bolt of cloth in Ostavia (6 ÷ 6)
Ostavia has the comparative advantage in rice, because its opportunity cost is lower

parts.sample: In Castrel, 1 ton of rice costs $8 \div 4 = 2$ bolts of cloth; in Ostavia it costs $6 \div 6 = 1$ bolt. Ostavia gives up less cloth for each ton, so Ostavia has the comparative advantage in rice, and Castrel will tend to import rice.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Castrel opens to trade, and the world price of rice is \$4 a ton. Draw a correctly labeled graph of Castrel's rice market and show the world price.

slips.PW: Castrel's own price is \$7; a world price of \$4 sits below the domestic equilibrium.

rubric.point: A correctly labeled graph: price and quantity axes, downward-sloping domestic demand and upward-sloping domestic supply
accept: P and Q axes with D and S labeled

rubric.point: A horizontal world price line (PW) below the domestic equilibrium price

parts.sample: Vertical axis: Price; horizontal axis: Quantity of rice. Domestic demand D slopes down and domestic supply S slopes up, crossing at \$7 and 50 tons. A horizontal line labeled PW is drawn at \$4, below that crossing.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Shade the area that represents consumer surplus in Castrel at the world price.

slips.cs-before: That is consumer surplus without trade. At the lower world price, buyers gain the area under demand above PW.

rubric.point: Shades the area under demand and above the world price, out to the quantity demanded at the world price
accept: the triangle under D above PW

parts.sample: Consumer surplus is the triangle under the demand curve and above the world price line, from zero out to the quantity demanded at the world price.

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: Using the table, calculate Castrel's rice imports per day at the world price. Show your work.

rubric.point: 60 tons, with work: 80 demanded minus 20 supplied at \$4

parts.sample: At \$4, Castrel demands 80 tons and its farms supply 20, so imports are $80 - 20 = 60$ tons a day.

parts.label: E
parts.prompt: Castrel then places a tariff of \$1 a ton on imported rice, so rice sells in Castrel for \$5. Calculate the tariff revenue per day. Show your work.

rubric.point: \$40, with work: \$1 times the imports after the tariff, 70 − 30 = 40 tons

parts.sample: At \$5, imports are $70 - 30 = 40$ tons. Tariff revenue = $\$1 \times 40 = \$40$ a day.

parts.label: F
parts.prompt: Shade the deadweight loss caused by the tariff.

slips.tariff-revenue: That rectangle is the tariff revenue, collected by the government; the deadweight loss is the two triangles beside it.

rubric.point: Shades both triangles: between supply and the world price from the old to the new domestic output, and between demand and the world price from the new to the old quantity demanded

parts.sample: Two triangles: one bounded by the supply curve and the world price line between the domestic output at PW and at PW + t, and one bounded by the demand curve and the world price line between the quantity demanded at PW + t and at PW.

parts.label: G
parts.prompt: Identify the effect of the tariff on each of the following in Castrel, compared with free trade at \$4: (i) producer surplus of Castrel's rice farms; (ii) consumer surplus.

rubric.point: Producer surplus increases (domestic farms sell more at a higher price)
Consumer surplus decreases (buyers pay more and buy less)

parts.sample: (i) Producer surplus increases: Castrel's farms sell 30 tons instead of 20 at \$5 instead of \$4. (ii) Consumer surplus decreases: buyers pay \$5 instead of \$4 and buy 70 tons instead of 80.
